p: DOSSIER_STATE_PROSE_POWER.DS-POW-7.pools.receipt deferred (the alignment exists and has not happened)[1].angle
DOSSIER_STATE_PROSE_POWER.DS-POW-7.pools.receipt deferred (the alignment exists and has not happened)[1].text
text: {settlement} already holds three combinations, and a fourth alignment is being held at the cap rather than refused. The houses concerned are aligned in everything but form.

p: DOSSIER_STATE_PROSE_POWER.DS-POW-7.pools.receipt deferred (the alignment exists and has not happened)[2].text
text: {faction} outbid the combination for {counterpart}'s seat at {settlement}, and the alignment that would have formed did not.

p: DOSSIER_STATE_PROSE_POWER.DS-POW-7.pools.hostile leader tie HARD-BLOCKS an otherwise natural alignment[0].angle
DOSSIER_STATE_PROSE_POWER.DS-POW-7.pools.hostile leader tie HARD-BLOCKS an otherwise natural alignment[0].text
text: Two houses at {settlement} want the same things and will not sit together; what is between the people at the head of them is bitter enough that the interests do not get a hearing.

p: DOSSIER_STATE_PROSE_POWER.DS-POW-7.pools.hostile leader tie HARD-BLOCKS an otherwise natural alignment[1].text
text: The obvious alliance at {settlement} does not happen, and the town knows exactly whose quarrel is preventing it.

p: DOSSIER_STATE_PROSE_POWER.DS-POW-7.pools.hostile leader tie HARD-BLOCKS an otherwise natural alignment[2].text
text: The interests of {faction} and {counterpart} at {settlement} coincide almost exactly and the two do not sit together; the block is personal, and it holds harder than any policy would.

p: DOSSIER_STATE_PROSE_POWER.DS-POW-7.pools.an opposition bloc forms COVERT under an autarchy[0].text
text: There is an alignment against the {seat} at {settlement} and it is not a bloc, it is a conspiracy. Under this kind of rule there is no other form it could take.

p: DOSSIER_STATE_PROSE_POWER.DS-POW-7.pools.an opposition bloc forms COVERT under an autarchy[1].text
text: Seats at {settlement} are coordinating where they cannot be seen to, which is slower, smaller and a great deal more dangerous than coordinating openly.

p: DOSSIER_STATE_PROSE_POWER.DS-POW-7.pools.an opposition bloc forms COVERT under an autarchy[2].text
text: There are meetings at {settlement} that are not meetings, held by people who have no reason to be in the same room and are anyway.
DS-STR-1: Overview › Active crisis banners · `settlement.stress[] {type, icon, label, colour, summary, crisisHook}`
Nothing moves through the gates. {settlement} lives on what is already inside the walls, and counts it daily.
The walls are held from outside; the fields beyond them have not been worked since the lines closed.
Trade stops at the gate rather than the market now. The siege decides what the town eats.
{settlement} is shut, and the shutting is not the town's decision; every arrangement inside the walls has been rebuilt around the gates staying closed.
{settlement}'s stores are being counted daily and issued against a list, and the list is shorter than the town.
Nobody goes in or out of {settlement}, and the walls have people on them at hours walls do not normally have people on them.
There is not enough to eat, and the shortfall is public now rather than private. The granary answers fewer hands each week.
Hunger has moved from the poorest streets into the ordinary ones; what the fields returned does not reach the table.
The market has grain, and the price of it has become a kind of politics; families are eating stores meant for {season}.
There is not enough food in {settlement} and there is no longer a polite way to discuss it.
What {settlement}'s granary holds is being issued by rule rather than by price, and the rule is being tested.
{settlement}'s market is open and thin, and the thinness is not seasonal.
Another power's writ runs here. The offices are the same offices; the authority behind them is not.
Revenue leaves before it is spent: {settlement} is administered, and the administration is not its own.
The garrison is quartered inside the walls, and the town's business is conducted around it.
{settlement} is held by somebody it did not choose, and the town's own hall now advises rather than decides.
Every licence, levy and permission in {settlement} passes a hand that is not the town's before it takes effect.
{settlement} functions and it functions under supervision, and the supervision is not disguised.
Nothing is decided. The factions each hold enough to block and none hold enough to rule, so the work of governing sits unattended.
Authority here is divided past the point of use. Repairs, judgments and appointments all wait on a consensus that does not arrive.
The town is governed in pieces, and the pieces do not agree; deferral has become the only policy anyone can pass.
{settlement} has no single answer to anything, because there is no longer anyone entitled to give one.
Two sets of instructions circulate in {settlement} and the clerks have quietly decided which to obey.
Asking {settlement} a simple question gets a careful one back, because the answer depends on who is asking for whom.
A share of everything {settlement} earns leaves for a creditor beyond the walls, and the share is not small.
The books balance only because nothing is being built. The debt is served first and the town second.
The obligation is outside and the payment is here; coin that would have gone to the works goes to the collector.
{settlement}'s obligations exceed what its year produces, and the shortfall is being met by promising against the next one.
What {settlement} owes is the first thing paid and the last thing discussed.
{settlement} looks like it is working hard for somebody, and the somebody is not in the town.
Trust here is a shorter commodity than it was. Institutions run at partial strength because too few people will vouch for one another.
The betrayal is over and its consequences are not. Offices that once shared information now keep it.
{settlement} works, but it works suspiciously; the arrangements that depended on good faith have quietly lapsed.
{settlement} was let down by somebody it had reason to trust, and the town has grown careful in a way that reaches past the person responsible.
Agreements at {settlement} are being written longer than they used to be written, and the length is the town's answer.
{settlement} deals fairly with a stranger and slowly, and the slowness is deliberate.
Nothing here looks wrong. Decisions land slightly askew, and information reaches the wrong hands slightly too often.
The economy is untouched and the intelligence is not. Someone else's interest is being served inside the town's own rooms.
There is no visible crisis. The pattern is legible only to whoever is counting the coincidences.
Somebody in {settlement} answers elsewhere, and the town knows it without knowing who.
What {settlement}'s hall discusses and what {settlement}'s hall records have come apart.
Conversation in {settlement} stops when it should not and resumes carefully.
Illness is loose in the town. The market thins as people keep to their own doors, and travel is discouraged rather than forbidden.
The sick outnumber the hands that can tend them, and the quarantine is observed unevenly, street by street.
{settlement} has stopped moving at its ordinary speed: supply arrives late, work goes undone, and the healers are the busiest people here.
Sickness has come into {settlement}, and the town has begun organising itself around containment rather than around work.
{settlement} is keeping two lists now (the sick and the exposed), and neither list is shrinking.
Doors in {settlement} are marked, and the marking is recent enough that people still look at it.
The seat is empty and no claim has settled. Major decisions are deferred; the institutions carry on under their own momentum.
There is no one to sign, so nothing is signed. Several offices have simply begun deciding for themselves.
Authority here has no undisputed heir, and the vacancy is being filled unofficially by whoever stands nearest the work.
The seat at {settlement} is empty and nobody has been able to say for certain who should fill it.
Instructions from {settlement}'s hall have stopped being signed, because there is nobody with the standing to sign them.
{settlement} answers questions about its own governance in the past tense.
The roads outside are not safe. Trade arrives thinner and later, and what the town does not spend on defense it does not have.
Attacks on the outlying holdings have become regular enough to plan around, and the plans cost coin the town was spending elsewhere.
{settlement} keeps more watch than it can afford; the country beyond the walls has stopped being ordinary country.
Something in the country around {settlement} has made the outlying work dangerous, and the outlying work is not optional.
{settlement} has pulled its stock and its people inward, and the ground it has given up is on the rolls as abandoned.
The fields furthest from {settlement} are standing untended, and nothing about the season explains it.
An armed movement operates inside the town's own population, and the town cannot tell it from the town.
Order here is enforced rather than kept. The authority that answers force with force is losing the argument that matters.
Parts of {settlement} are governed by the consent of people who hold no office; the rest is governed nervously.
Part of {settlement} is fighting the rest of it and neither part wears a badge.
The watch's patrols at {settlement} have been rewritten, and the routes now avoid places rather than cover them.
{settlement} is calm in a way that a stranger will not be able to trust for long.
The town's creed is contested from within. Congregations that once shared a calendar now keep separate ones.
A rival observance has taken root deep enough to divide households. The old rite still holds the buildings and no longer holds the street.
Faith here has become a question of allegiance rather than habit, and the question is being asked out loud.
What {settlement} keeps has changed, and the households have not all changed at the same rate.
{settlement}'s observances are being kept twice (in the new form publicly, in the old form otherwise), and the clerks record only one of them.
The altars in {settlement} are tended and the tending is new, which is visible in the stonework.
The bound labour of {settlement} has stopped being reliable, and the settlement was built on its reliability.
The work is not being done and the refusal is organized. What held the arrangement together was never consent.
The overseers keep order in the daylight hours; what happens after them is no longer theirs to decide.
The people {settlement} held have stopped being held, and the town has no arrangement for what follows.
{settlement}'s rolls are wrong in a way the clerks cannot correct: the names are there and the people are not where the names say.
{settlement} is a town with two populations and one of them has stopped pretending.
The town is on a war footing. Grain, iron and men are counted against a campaign rather than a season.
{settlement} lives at the rhythm of a war it is part of. Everything ordinary is scheduled around the levy.
The trades that matter here now are the ones that supply an army; the rest have been asked to wait.
{settlement} is at war, and the war has reached the town as absence: the men, the carts, and the ordinary expectation of next year.
{settlement}'s levies and requisitions have become the largest single line in the year, and they are not negotiable.
{settlement} is short of the kind of people a town this size should be full of.
People are arriving faster than the town can house them. The camps outside the wall are becoming a second settlement.
{settlement} has more mouths than arrangements. The administration is improvising, and the improvisation is visible.
The newcomers came from somewhere worse, and their arrival is reshaping what the town can afford.
People have come into {settlement} in numbers the town did not plan for, and the planning is happening after the fact.
{settlement}'s rolls have grown by {band} and its housing has not grown at all.
There are more people in {settlement} than there is {settlement}, and the overflow is visible at the edges.
{settlement} is carrying more than one crisis at once, and they are not independent. Each makes the others harder to end.
No single emergency explains the state of the town; the troubles here compound, and the compounding is the real condition.
The town has run out of the slack it would need to solve any one of its problems, because it is solving several.
{settlement} carries no emergency. What troubles it are the ordinary troubles, and they are being handled at the ordinary pace.
Nothing here is urgent. The town's difficulties are chronic rather than acute, and it has the room to work on them.
There is no crisis on the books. Whatever strain the settlement carries, it carries at a weight it can hold.

The trouble is new here. It shows in small displacements (a schedule slipping, a price moving) and has not yet been named out loud.

This is the worst of it. The strain has stopped compounding and started simply holding at a level nothing here was built for.
The pressure is at its height. What is going to survive this part is surviving it; what is not is failing now.

{settlement} has what this crisis requires and has it in the right combination; recovery here is a schedule rather than a hope.
Every leg the town needed, it has. That is rarer than it sounds, and it is why this is ending sooner than it began.

{settlement} has resources against this and not the full set. The missing leg means its strengths hold rather than push.
The response here is adequate without being decisive. One gap is enough to turn a recovery into an endurance.
What is carrying {settlement} through this is {reason}. The rest of the town's strengths are following that one.
The recovery here rests on {reason}, which is doing more work than anyone sized it for.
{reason} is why this has not been worse. Take it out and the arithmetic is a different arithmetic.
The town has little to bring against this. It will end when it ends, and not because of anything {settlement} does.
There is no lever here. The strengths that would shorten this crisis are the strengths the town does not have.
{settlement} is enduring rather than resisting. The trouble decays at its own pace, and the town waits it out.
Hunger and sickness are compounding here. The ill cannot work the fields, and the fields are why they are ill.
The two troubles feed each other: what the sickness takes from the harvest, the shortfall returns to the sickbeds.
{settlement} is short of food and short of the health to grow it, and neither shortage lifts before the other.
The hunger cannot lift while the lines hold. Relief exists; it is simply on the wrong side of the walls.
There is grain within a short road of here and none of it can reach the town. The shortage ends when the siege does, and not before.
This famine is not a failure of harvest. It is a blockade, and it keeps exactly as long as the blockade keeps.
The resistance is bleeding the garrison. Occupation and revolt feed each other here, and the arrangement costs the occupier more each season.
{settlement} is held and it is fighting; the holding is expensive in a way that is shortening it.
The occupation made the resistance and the resistance is unmaking the occupation: an ugly equilibrium, and an expensive one for whoever is paying to hold it.

{settlement} owes coin it could have paid before the market turned; each week the obligation grows against the means.

This was paid for elsewhere. {settlement} is the place it happens, not the place it was decided.

The pressure on {settlement} comes from a named and openly hostile neighbour; there is nothing to uncover, only something to answer.

{settlement} is occupied and it is fighting back; what runs in the alleys is organized, patient, and not interested in reform.

DS-CND-1: Active conditions: severity, direction, provenance and family · `settlement.activeConditions[] {archetype, severity, severityBand, status, triggeredAt, duration, causes[], affectedSystems[]}`
