Rented storage where merchants hold goods between arrival and sale. The backbone of any settlement that lives by the trade route.
A posting house for paid help: torchbearers, porters, guides, and other non-combatants hired by the day or the job.
Tellers of fortunes who trade in cold reading and showmanship rather than real divination. Cheap, convincing, and entirely mundane.
Handlers who break and train common animals for work, hunting, and war. Horses, hounds, and hawks, nothing exotic.
Rival chartered guilds that broker bounties, verify claims, and take a cut of what wanderers haul back. Competition keeps their rates honest and their rivalries loud.
A district given over to organized sellsword companies, from escort outfits to field regiments available for hire.
A cluster of outfitters specializing in gear for the deep places: rope, light, warding charms, and weapons that bite what ordinary steel cannot.
A quiet district of scholars, researchers, and keepers of obscure knowledge who sell answers to those who can afford the time.
A villager who works iron between farm chores, mending tools and shoeing horses. Good enough for the ordinary, rarely for the fine.
A part-time woodworker who frames buildings and mends carts alongside other labour. The first hand called when timber needs joining.
A rough shore landing with racks for drying and salting the catch. Where a waterside settlement turns fish into food and trade.
A gathering place where hunters pool game, pelts, and knowledge of the surrounding wild. Keeps the paths, the seasons, and the dangerous beasts in living memory.
A woodland trade that slow-burns timber into charcoal, the hot clean fuel a forge and a bakery cannot do without.
A tradesman who steeps and dries grain into malt, the raw material of ale. The brewer's necessary supplier.
A seasonal trade cutting and drying peat from the marsh for winter fuel. Poor country's answer to firewood.
A working yard where travellers leave and hire horses, with fodder, farriery, and a hand who knows the roads.
A shallow surface working that scrapes ore, coal, or stone from the ground. Hard, dirty labour for the poorest hands.
A worked face where crews cut and dress building stone. Slow, heavy work that supplies every wall and foundation for miles.
A dealer in mules, donkeys, and draft beasts who also hires out load-carriers to those bound for the road.
A holder of cattle or goats kept for milk, butter, and cheese. A steady source of fat and protein when grain runs short.
A keeper of flocks who moves sheep between winter and summer pasture for wool and meat. The textile trade begins at the shepherd's crook.
A works that evaporates brine into salt, the preservative that keeps meat and fish through the lean season. Viable only near flats or salt springs.
A water or wind mill that grinds the district's grain, usually under a monopoly. The miller holds a chokehold on bread and is resented for it.
A full-time worker of iron who forges and mends the tools, fittings, and blades a community runs on.
A full-time woodworker who raises houses, builds carts, and makes furniture. Present wherever timber is worked in earnest.
A roofer who lays and mends thatch, the common covering for house and barn. Skilled work that keeps the weather out.
A maker of barrels, casks, and tubs. Nothing is stored or shipped in bulk without the cooper's watertight staves.
A seller of herbal remedies, poultices, and common cures who works no magic. Knows which roots heal and which mushrooms kill.
A craftsman who makes bows, crossbows, and arrows and stocks finished shafts by the sheaf. First stop for an empty quiver.
A powered saw that turns logs into planks and beams, feeding the building and furniture trades faster than any pit-saw.
An organized shaft or excavation drawing ore, coal, or stone from deposits. Needs capital and coordination a small settlement cannot muster.
A works that turns raw hides into leather with bark and lime. Foul-smelling, and sited downstream and downwind where the water and the ground allow.
A finisher who cleans and thickens woven cloth, often by water power, turning loose weave into hard-wearing fabric.
A tradesman who colours cloth and yarn. Without the dyer, everything stays the grey of undyed wool.
A maker of fired clay vessels for the kitchen and store: plates, jugs, and crocks turned on the wheel and baked in a kiln.
A moulder and firer of clay bricks, the material of permanent building. Needs good clay and steady fuel.
A brewer of ale in quantity for alehouses and households. After the baker, the largest buyer of grain in any town.
A keeper of stabling who trains and boards horses for riding and draft. Essential to any settlement on a road.
A keeper of hives for honey and beeswax. Honey sweetens the table, and wax makes candles, seals, and polish.
A dealer who buys, salts, and sells fish, standing between the boats and the table. Fresh near water, cured inland.
A maker and mender of shoes and boots. Steady, universal work, since every person needs something on their feet.
A cutter and sewer of garments from finished cloth, serving the middling sort between home needle and master clothier.
The attendant at births who manages hard labours and tends new mothers. The most used healer in any community.
One of the few who can read and write, hired to copy letters, draft contracts, and read documents aloud for the unlettered.
A hunter of ducks, geese, and marsh birds with net, trap, and trained fowl, supplying the market with feathered game.
A carver who shapes wood into tool handles, furniture, and sacred figures. Handles both the useful and the devotional.
A workshop that draws and sells maps, from road charts to rough sketches of the wild. Rare enough that most places have none.
Several mills grinding grain and fulling cloth, the sign of a settlement large enough to need more than one wheel.
Several smiths, some specialized, working iron for a whole town's tools, fittings, and arms.
A body of woodworkers handling a town's construction and furniture at a scale beyond any single hand.
Cloth-makers, often guild-organized, turning spun fibre into woven fabric for local use and trade.
Leatherworkers who cure hides at scale. Their reek pushes them toward the downstream edge, where the town can spare the ground.
Regulated slaughterers and meat-sellers who dress carcasses and supply the market under strict rules of cleanliness.
Guild-regulated bakers who bake the town's daily bread at fixed weights and prices.
A proper apothecary's shop with trained staff, stocked shelves, and a back room for consultations. Some also set bones and dress wounds.
A guild of bow and arrow makers producing ammunition by the sheaf and arms to commission. Restocks caravans and outfits militias.
A furnace works that refines raw ore into workable metal, the industrial step between the mine and the smithy.
A commercial powered mill cutting planks and beams for the building trade at regional scale, with a permanent crew.
A commercial brewhouse supplying taverns and regional trade. A major employer and a heavy consumer of grain.
A full tannery with many vats and trained hands, producing quality leather for footwear, armour, and harness.
An organized body of shoemakers producing footwear for a whole town under regulated standards.
A guild of master clothiers turning finished cloth into everything from work clothes to livery.
A maker of candles, soap, and rope from tallow and similar stock. The trade that keeps a town lit and clean.
A worker of molten glass into bottles, panes, and vessels. Needs fine sand, potash, and a skilled hand at the furnace.
A chartered works that strikes refined metal into standard coin. A licence from the crown or a lord and a steady source of revenue.
The official voice of the town, calling proclamations, prices, and news in the square at set hours.
A twister of fibre into rope and cordage, indispensable to ships, building sites, and farms alike.
Separate guilds of armourers, swordsmiths, and jewellers whose fine metalwork goes beyond the common smith.
A district trading in silks, spices, and precious goods for those with coin to burn.
A press turning out books and broadsheets in numbers no scribe could match, where the craft is known.
Skilled makers of windows, vessels, and mirrors. Demanding work that only a sizable centre can support.
A guild for nearly every conceivable trade, the mark of a great city where specialization has run to its limit.
Someone who quietly buys goods without asking their origin. Everyone knows who; no one says it aloud.
A discreet arrangement that hides people who need to disappear. A barn, a cellar, and a habit of not asking.
A buyer of stolen goods known by face rather than name, through whom hot property moves without a word written down.
A household or two tied to the bandits who work the surrounding roads, trading shelter and information for a share.
A stop where goods pass to dodge tolls and customs, paid for in a cut of the cargo.
A run of quiet hands moving a particular commodity past tolls and inspection. Usually built around one lucrative good.
An organized band of pickpockets and toughs who claim a patch of streets and take their tribute from it.
An organized trade in untaxed and illicit goods that lives on evading the customs house.
Legitimate-looking shops and trades that launder coin and cover for what really pays the rent.
A chartered chapter of organized theft that regulates its members, fences their takings, and enforces its own law.
Rival gangs contesting the same streets, whose turf disputes spill into open violence.
A hidden trade in contraband and forbidden goods, meeting where the watch does not look.
A dug warren of tunnels and cellars beneath the settlement, used for discreet passage, untaxed storage, and no-questions transport. Everyone knows it exists; no one holds a map.
A lone killer or small cell working below the notice of any guild, hired through criminal go-betweens. Deniable and never reliable.
A crew that seizes free people and sells them on with forged papers, feeding whatever market will take them.
A clandestine operation moving people across borders outside all law, with its own safe houses and bought officials.
A dominant criminal syndicate tolerated because open gang war would be worse. It taxes crime and keeps it quiet.
A permanent underground market for contraband, forged documents, and services no lawful trade will touch.
A licensed house that pays for road news and keeps the register of who arrived, from where, and carrying word of what. It exists wherever traffic does.

The guild form of the listening house, with paid correspondents on several roads and an archive that checks one road against another. The only counter in the city where a claim is graded before it is sold.
A loft of message birds run by people who file no returns. Word arrives unsigned and ahead of the watch, and only a standing criminal organization can keep a loft like it safe.
A covert guild of brokers who buy and sell knowledge by the piece, grade what they sell, and will build a claim for a patron who pays enough. It sites itself among the fences and the late houses.
Repurposed tunnels and catacombs sheltering criminals, refugees, and everything that needs to stay out of daylight.
A professional order of killers working through cut-outs and cover, acknowledged by no one and used by many.
Ordinary residents who drill and muster against local threats. Part-time soldiers with their own tools and no pay.
One able-bodied adult from each household musters with hunting bows, spears, and farm tools when danger reaches the fields.
A wooden palisade or earthen bank thrown up to slow raiders and beasts. Rough defence for a place that cannot afford stone.
A drinking hall for old soldiers and mercenaries. Informal muscle, tall tales, and the occasional job for a band that needs swords.
Stone walls and gates ringing a town. Costly to raise and costly to keep, but they decide who gets in.
Part-time guards who walk the night and hold the gates. Keepers of order rather than a fighting force.
Controlled entry points in the wall, manned by gatekeepers who decide what passes and what waits outside.
Quarters for the town's guards or a small garrison. Where the armed hand of the settlement sleeps and eats.
A billet and contracting office for professional soldiers between campaigns. Trained men who fight in formation for wages, not plunder.
Masonry walls with towers and gatehouses ringing a city. The single largest thing most cities ever build.
A full-time force that polices a city day and night, roughly one in a hundred of its people under arms.
Professional soldiers kept under a noble or royal banner, stationed to hold a place against real armies.
An inner fortress and last refuge, built to hold when the outer walls have fallen.
Layered wall systems with outer rings, inner keep, and distributed garrisons. A metropolis armoured against the age of siege.
Soldiers stationed in separate quarters, because no single barracks can hold a city this size.
No mill of its own; the grain is carried to a manor or village wheel, often under a lord's monopoly.
Households farming just enough to feed themselves, with little or nothing left to trade.
A settlement whose living comes off the water, built around nets, traps, and drying racks.
A community that manages its flocks in common and moves to the rhythm of the grazing calendar.
A seasonal camp felling and stacking timber. The whole place runs on the cut and the haul.
Ale brewed and sold from a back room, doubling as the gathering place where news and disputes are settled.
A room over the stable and a hot meal for those passing through. It exists only because the road does.
A walled waystation offering water, fodder, and safe lodging to merchants and their animals. Without one, hard country cannot be crossed.
An occasional trading day held by habit rather than charter, on any flat ground that will hold a crowd.
A lender against pledged goods at steep interest and no questions. Often the only credit a poor household can find.
Shared pasture held in common, where the community's livestock feed.
Open-field farmland worked in rotation, the ordinary agricultural base of a settled village.
A single inn with rooms, stabling, and a common meal for traders and pilgrims on the road.
A chartered market held once a week where the district buys and sells its produce and goods.
A household brew sold on the premises, most often by the women who make it.
A flat ferry and the family that has held the crossing rights for generations. The short way over water for those who will pay.
A yard that builds and mends shallow river craft: barges, punts, and ferries fitted for flat water.
A stall or small covered market selling the day's catch, where prices fall fast because fish will not wait.
A bridge with a toll house whose keeper takes passage fees and does the small repairs. Minor but steady coin.
A fortified overnight stop with stabling, water, and provisions, built for caravans and loaded wagons rather than comfort.
Communal grain storage that buffers the harvest and holds off famine in a bad year.
The central plaza where weekly markets and fairs are held, the commercial heart of a town.
A yearly gathering that draws regional merchants and luxury goods a weekly market never sees.
A handful of merchant guilds that control trade in particular goods and set their own terms.
Guilds that regulate quality, prices, and apprenticeship across a town's trades.
Dealers who exchange foreign coin and lend at interest, the seed of banking in a growing town.
Several inns lodging the traders who pass through, a sign of real traffic on the roads.
A spread of drinking houses that serve as the everyday social hubs of a busy town.
River or coastal docks for loading bulk cargo. The gateway for anything that moves by water.
A guild of professional carters and teamsters who move goods overland for hire and know every road and toll.
A road inn built around relay horses and scheduled coaches, with fixed meals and a room for waiting passengers.
A communal bathing house with heated water. A social hub in some cultures, a suspect one in others, and the best place for rumour in either.
A yard where carters and pack-drivers are hired for the road, and returning ones trade news of its conditions.
A yard that builds and repairs seagoing merchant ships. A heavy investment demanding timber, iron, and shipwrights.
A public auction of enslaved people, run openly where the law permits it as ordinary commercial business.
An office that tests the purity of precious metal for a fee. Necessary groundwork for banking and coinage.
The office that levies duties on goods moving through the port and roads, run by royal or town officials.
A stable of relay horses that carries letters and small packages faster than any traveller on foot.
A quarter of concentrated stabling, horse trading, and farriery serving merchants, soldiers, and riders.
A post that assembles caravans, sets departures, and sells route intelligence. The town-scale forerunner of a city's caravan exchange.
A worker of precious metal and gems into rings, seals, and finery, who also appraises stones and sometimes buys quiet goods.
A maker and cellarer of wine, selling in bulk to taverns and by the bottle to the wealthy. Inland, an importer and blender.
Multiple large, state-managed grain stores that feed a city and hold against shortage.
Several permanent market squares serving different districts of a large city.
Markets that trade every day in several places at once, the mark of a true urban economy.
Whole districts of inns and taverns catering to merchants, travellers, and long-staying visitors.
Great fairs drawing international merchants where letters of credit change hands alongside goods.
Houses that lend, exchange coin, and issue letters of credit. Real banking, viable only at city scale.
Powerful merchant guilds whose reach makes them a political force in city affairs.
Guilds of extreme specialization, down to the gold-beater and the mirror-maker.
A district of warehouses holding merchant goods between shipment and sale.
A company running a fleet of river barges on set and hired routes, carrying bulk cargo, passengers, and supply.
Permanent offices where caravan masters, merchants, and armed escorts do business: bonded freight, route news, and convoy assembly.
A licensed district for commerce in people, with auction halls, holding compounds, and the brokers and clerks that serve them.
A guild producing the region's most accurate maps and charts, off the shelf or to commission.
A cluster of competing apothecaries whose rivalry breeds specialists in surgery, herbs, and imported medicine.
A chartered mint striking standard coin for a region, and a steady source of revenue for the authority behind it.
A formal venue for selling high-value goods: estates, ships, art, livestock, and occasionally people, all on a premium.
The office that governs navigable-water traffic: berths, anchorage fees, manifests, and port law.
A quarter of fur processors and traders dealing in a high-value luxury good.
Several specialized market districts, each given over to one thing: grain, cloth, metals, livestock, or exotica.
Dozens of merchant guilds forming, in effect, a parliament of trade.
A whole financial quarter of international banks, letters of credit, and currency speculation at scale.
A hub for foreign merchant houses, trade arbitration, and commodity exchange.
A state-run network of granaries holding strategic reserves against war and famine.
Bards, jugglers, and acrobats who arrive for the fairs and move on when they end.
A back-room trade in dice, cards, and small games of chance, and the debts they breed.
A school that trains fighters for the arena, drawing on prisoners, debtors, and the desperate. It feeds the blood-sport circuit.
Professional fighters for private hire: bodyguard work, debt collection, and the quiet removal of problems.
A tolerated or regulated house of prostitution.
Permanent venues for staged performance, the sign of a city with leisure and coin to spend on it.
Dedicated houses of chance, some licensed and some not, where fortunes turn on a roll.
A tolerated quarter of prostitution set apart from respectable trade.
Underground venues for illegal or barely-legal blood sport, hidden from the authorities that would close them.
Several standing theatres worked by professional companies, a mark of urban culture.
A great arena for gladiatorial games and beast fights, staged at a scale meant to awe a whole city.
A large, organized quarter given over to the sex trade.
A concentration of gaming houses, run under whatever oaths and enforcement keep the play honest.
A venue of high culture and elite patronage, where wealth displays itself as much as the performance.
A formal school of music and performance, with an amphitheatre and dormitories, viable only in a large city.
Merchants dealing in goods from other planes of existence, where such traffic is possible.
An ancient wyrm dwelling within the city, whose presence shapes its politics, its fears, and its fortunes.
Constructed servants doing the labour of many, where magic permits their making.
Animated corpses set to work. Efficient, tireless, and deeply divisive wherever it is practised.
Parlours selling shared and lucid dreams through high magic, for experience or for private communion.
Mooring towers with warded weather protection for airships, the infrastructure of a sky-trading power.
A network of paired speaking stones carrying words across great distance for a fee.
The eldest or most respected residents guide shared decisions by consensus, without office or title.
Every household head holds an equal voice on common matters. Slower to decide, but broadly shared.
A steward set over the settlement by a distant lord to collect and oversee. His authority is real and often resented.
One household head speaks for the settlement by common acknowledgement, with no formal appointment behind it.
A lord's agent who manages the land, gathers rents, and enforces noble authority on the ground.
A single respected figure who acts as authority by acknowledgement rather than election. Decisions are practical, not formal.
An officer chosen from the peasantry who organizes labour, settles disputes, and answers to outside authority for the village.
The oldest or most respected resident who guides decisions where no formal office exists.
Elected or appointed leadership governing a town's civic affairs.
The guilds run the town, with guildmasters seated on the council and trade interests setting policy.
An official placed by a lord to govern, whose noble mandate overrides local custom.
An informal council of prominent citizens managing town affairs where no chartered government exists.
A consortium of guild masters holding effective civic power over a city.
A royal or ducal appointee governing the city as a noble fief.
Wealthy merchant families holding civic power, where office is effectively bought.
A city that governs itself and its territory as an independent polity, owing no higher lord.
A citizen assembly holding formal authority, debating and voting on the city's major questions.
A city administered directly for the crown by a governor or viceroy. High status and high scrutiny.
A working apparatus of officials, clerks, and ward officers running city affairs by bureaucratic routine.
The seat of state government, with palace, ministries, and audience halls in one great complex.
Separate courts, commercial, criminal, appellate, and religious, sitting at once in a great city.
A cluster of simple homes in wattle and timber, a room or two to a household.
The well or spring the settlement drinks from. Everything else depends on it.
A ring of sharpened stakes offering the least defence that still deters a casual raider.
A shared underground store for grain, roots, and preserved food. The buffer that carries a place through a bad harvest.
Timber-framed, thatch-roofed homes, the housing stock of a small growing settlement.
Wells and springs spread through the settlement, so no single failure leaves it dry.
Timber homes on stone foundations, the housing of an established village.
A meeting place and administrative centre where a town's civic business is done.
A borough court where local justice is heard and judgement handed down.
Holding cells and public stocks for the town's offenders. Confinement and open shame in one.
Multi-storey timber and stone housing packed for a town's growing population.
An imposing civic building that houses a city's government and announces its importance.
Separate commercial, criminal, and religious courts, because one bench cannot hear a city's business.
A sizable gaol holding debtors, criminals, and political prisoners together.
A house where the able-bodied poor are given shelter and food in return for hard, compulsory labour. Kept deliberately harsh to discourage dependence.
Underground drainage carrying waste away from the streets. Rare, costly, and worth more than its cost in lives.
Dense multi-storey housing and tenements packing a city's population, poorest at the bottom.
Engineered conduits, cisterns, and fountains bringing clean water into a city from beyond it.
A state prison complex holding political prisoners, debtors, and criminals in separate wards.
Multiple aqueducts, cisterns, and fountains managing a metropolis's water at scale.
A wandering caster of the simplest spells who passes through now and then. Present only in passing.
A rough hall under a regional adventuring charter that posts bounties, shelters monster hunters, and rallies defence when the garrison cannot. Common on hard frontiers.
A resident caster of modest power who handles the small magics a community occasionally needs.
A circle of druids bound to the land who mind the seasons, the clean streams, and the peace with wild things.
A resident able to mend wounds and sickness through modest divine healing. Rare and valued where it is found.
The residence and workshop of a single wizard of real ability, viable only where a place is large enough to want one.
A council of senior druids that governs their circle's dealings with a city, tending hidden groves and speaking for wild places.
A shop selling potions and alchemical goods, from healing draughts to useful reagents.
A ranger station or druid waypost that watches the surrounding wild, keeps the trails, and turns scout in a crisis.
A rare permanent circle for instant travel, ruinously expensive to build and to keep working.
An organized body of spellcasters that trains, licenses, and polices the arcane within a city.
A quarter of alchemical workshops under guild organization, producing potions and compounds at scale.
A workshop that crafts magic items, viable only in a large and wealthy city.
A scribe who prepares and sells spell scrolls, from cheap charms to costly greater workings.
A formal institution of arcane learning with a full curriculum, research halls, and visiting scholars.
A whole quarter of arcane practitioners: towers, workshops, libraries, and reagent merchants.
The largest store of knowledge for a great distance, holding thousands of volumes and archives.
A standing diplomatic mission from a planar power, dealing in trade, intelligence, and the occasional intervention.
A simple prayer marker at the roadside with no resident clergy. A place to pause and ask for safe passage.
No church of its own; worshippers walk a few miles to the nearest village church for services.
The stone-built centre of village life, funded by mandatory tithes and marking every birth, marriage, and death.
A resident singer or piper who plays the festivals and weddings and carries local history in song.
The settlement's resident clergyman, who performs the rites, collects the tithe, and is often its only literate soul.
Consecrated ground about the church where the dead are laid.
A plot at the settlement edge where the dead are laid, kept by the households themselves rather than by any clergy.
Ground beside each parish church, with a sexton who keeps the register of who lies where.
Grounds outside the gates, and a house where bones are stacked when the old plots are lifted to make room.
Burial grounds beyond every gate, served by their own roads and answering to one central roll of the dead.
Several parish churches, each serving its own quarter of a town.
A religious community of monks or friars, often running a hospital or school alongside its devotions.
A modest house caring for the sick poor, almost always run by a religious order.
A charitable house sheltering the destitute, the aged, and the disabled who cannot work, funded by endowment and pious donation.
A bishop's seat and the mark of a major city, viable only where the population is large enough to sustain it.
Several monastic houses of different orders, each with its own rule and work.
A large facility caring for the sick poor, with beds by the score and religious backing.
A house that takes in abandoned infants and raises them until they can be placed or apprenticed. Often a wheel in the wall allows a child to be left unseen.
A parish church for every neighbourhood, so no one lives far from a bell.
Hundreds of parish churches across every district, the faith woven into each neighbourhood.
A metropolitan cathedral and the seat of the region's highest religious authority, drawing pilgrims from afar.
Several great monastic houses whose scholarly, contemplative, and charitable work runs at scale.
Multiple hospitals and infirmaries across a metropolis, organized medical care at population scale.
A house of care for the dying and the incurably ill poor, kept by the faithful. No one is turned away for want of coin.
A house that takes in parentless children and raises them until they can be apprenticed or placed. Order and mercy under the temple hand.
A free infirmary that tends the sick and injured poor without fee. Mercy made into a standing institution.
A ring where the desperate and the enslaved fight for a paying crowd. Blood for coin, rowdy and cruel.
A walled yard where those who cannot pay are worked until their debt is cleared. Sanctioned harshness, orderly and profitable.

What the neighbours have been shown
Word of it is only now reaching the roads.
The first whispers of it are only now on the roads.
Rumor of it has only just begun to travel.
Word of it is barely abroad, and only on the nearest roads.
It hangs on the brink and may break at any hour.
It stands poised on the edge and may break at any hour.
It hangs by a thread and could break at any moment.
It sits on a knife's edge, apt to break before long.
It is being felt hard {scope} now.
It is striking hard {scope} as we speak.
The weight of it falls hard {scope} now.
It bites hard {scope}, and none can miss it.
Its effects are being felt {scope} now.
The mark of it is on things {scope} now.
It has, for the present, run its course.
It has, for now, spent itself.
For the present, it has settled and gone quiet.
It has run its course, at least for the season.
In the end it came to nothing.
In the end, nothing came of it.
It amounted to nothing in the end.
Nothing came of it, when all was said.
It passed before it could take hold.
It faded before it could take hold.
It came to nothing before it could take root.
It slipped away before it ever took hold.
Word of the war moves along the front, and the town listens for the drums.
The matter of arms stands unsettled, and every ear is turned toward the marches.
News of the fighting passes hand to hand, and the watch keeps a wary eye on the road.
Word of the faith moves among the temples, and the people turn to hear it.
The matter of devotion stirs the congregation, and the priests weigh what it means.
News from the altars passes pew to pew, and the faithful mark it well.
Word of the trade moves along the market roads, and the guilds take note.
The matter of goods and coin stirs the merchants, and the caravan-masters listen close.
News of the markets passes stall to stall, and the town reckons its stores.
Word of the sickness moves along the roads, and the healers keep their anxious watch.
The matter of the plague hangs over the country, and every household marks it well.
Word of the disaster passes from mouth to mouth, and the country reckons what it has lost.
The matter of the calamity weighs on every hearth, and the elders are asked what it means.
Word of the moving of peoples runs along the roads, and the country counts the strangers at its gates.
The matter of the newcomers stirs every quarter, and the elders weigh what welcome to give.
Word of the struggle for power moves through the country, and every faction listens for its moment.
The matter of who rules unsettles the halls, and the country watches the seat of power closely.
Word of the grain sent to a hungry neighbour moves along the roads, and the town reckons the cost of its mercy.
The matter of relief given and relief refused passes hand to hand, and every larder is counted anew.
Word of the country's good fortune moves along the market roads, and the guilds reckon their gains.
The matter of the fat years stirs every hearth, and the careful weigh how long the plenty will hold.
Word of the changing memory of old deeds moves through the country, and neighbours reckon the debts of the past anew.
The matter of who owes whom and who was wronged stirs every hearth, and the ledger of old favours is weighed again.
News that the past is being read afresh passes hand to hand, and the country wonders what its old friendships truly meant.
Steel is drawn along the marches. The muster horns have not stopped since dawn.
Hear it and mark it: a war is gathering at the borders, and the levy is called to the walls.
The watchfires are doubled and the roads run thick with soldiers; the town braces for what is coming.
Grievance has hardened into muster, and the drums along the front will not be quieted.
The smiths work through the night at the whetstone, and every household is counted for the levy.
War-banners are unrolled in the market square, and the young men look to the marches with hard eyes.
The granaries are locked against a siege that has not come yet, and the walls are walked twice a night.
A quarrel between neighbours has grown teeth, and the country readies its pikes for the worst.
The blow has fallen; smoke stands where the watchfires were.
War has come in earnest. The fighting is upon the front, and the wounded are already carried back.
The clash is joined, and the town counts its dead before it counts the cost.
Steel has met steel at the front; what was feared is now simply true.
The fields are trampled and the barns emptied to feed the muster; the war eats everything it touches.
Fire runs along the border holdings, and the roads are choked with those fleeing the sword.
The levy marches out under grey banners, and the widows are made before the harvest is in.
The ford is held by force and lost by force, and the river runs foul below the crossing.
The banners are furled and the wounded carried home. This front, at least, goes quiet.
The fighting has ebbed; the drums are silent and the muster horns hung up at last.
Peace of a kind holds along the marches, and the levy may sleep in its own beds tonight.
The war has spent itself here. The roads are safe again, and the widows begin their mourning.
The gates stand open once more, and the plough is taken up where the pike was laid down.
A truce is cried in the square, and the smiths turn from spearheads back to ploughshares.
The garrison thins as the danger passes, and the walls are given back to the ivy.
The last of the wounded mend by the hearth, and the marches learn the taste of quiet again.
The threatened war never came to the sword; the levy stands down, grumbling.
The muster is dismissed. The threatened war never marched, and the horns fall quiet unblooded.
Whatever gathered at the borders has thought better of it; the walls are unmanned and the drums put away.
The alarm came to nothing. No steel was drawn, and the town returns to its plows.
The war-banners are rolled away unstained, and the whetstones go back to their pegs.
The feared army melted from the marches before a blow fell, and the country lets out its breath.
The quarrel cooled without bloodshed, and the pikes are stacked in the tithe-barn once more.

The term is kept as written, and the peace holds here.
The term is kept only barely; the strain of it shows, and grows.
The term is broken, and this seam of the peace has torn.
The tribute is paid on time, the wagons rolling as the treaty promised.

The promised wagons no longer come; the tribute has stopped, and the oath lies broken here.

The compelled banner has turned away; the forced allyship is renounced.

The cap on arms is thrown off, and the forbidden muster gathers in the open.

The garrison keeps the walls uneasily; the townsfolk chafe and stones are thrown.
The garrison is besieged in the very town it holds; the occupation is repudiated.

An army crosses into the other's internal quarrel; the pledge of non-intervention lies broken.

The conveyed town answers its new banner slowly, and the seller's old stewards have not all gone home.
The conveyed town has thrown off the banner it was sold under, and the deed is waste parchment.

The strangers' priests find the roads longer than they were, and the squares oddly empty when they arrive.
The doors are shut to the strangers' priests, and what was written about the rites is no longer kept.
The families cross as the compact allows, and the fields they clear are theirs to work.
The families still cross, but the crossing has grown slow and the welcome at the far end thin.
The crossings are closed and the compact of passage is dead; those already over are on their own.
The named house trades on the terms it was promised, and the tollmen wave its wagons through.
The named house still trades, but the tollmen find new reasons to count, and the counting takes all day.
The promised terms of trade are withdrawn; the named house pays what any stranger pays, or is turned away.
The named are let be; the lists are not read out, and men who were owed a rope walk to market unremarked.
The lists are not read out, but neither are they burned, and a pardoned man finds honest work harder to come by than he did.
The old lists are read out again, and the pardon is kept as though it had never been written.
The reckoning is kept: at the appointed term the ledgers close, the bonds are struck through, and no one is asked again for what was released.
The term comes and the ledgers close slowly; the bonds are struck through one by one, and some are found to have been copied out elsewhere first.
The appointed term passes with the ledgers still open, and what was to have been released is demanded in full.
The term is kept as written, and the peace holds here.

Statecraft §2.4 GIVE lane: warning an ally, priced by the SACRIFICE of the telling (strategic advantage spent + eyes exposed), not the value received. The intel-posture coupling lands with W-DOCTRINE.

Statecraft §2.4 SELL lane (W-DOCTRINE-2b): intelligence sold as a priced good between NON-INTIMATE parties (distinct from the warning GIVE lane), the SELLER'S lineage attached. Price = intelSalePrice (fidelity-discounted, stakes-scaled, CREDIBILITY-priced — a proven liar's product sells cheap). THE SELF-POLICING MARKET: a sale later proven false feeds a deception CredibilityDelta against the seller (informationStatecraft.intelSaleCredibilityDeltas) → its stock falls → its future sales price lower. Expressed entirely with the live credibility stock; the autonomous per-tick seller mover is deferred (design §8: no whisper-war hum). The DEMAND lane (peace disclosure terms) lands with W-PEACE.

LIVE (E1d, design A2): the MARKET TWIN, wired as the post-REFUSE BONDED FALL-THROUGH ("you won't give? I'll pay"). Grain conserves through the same sink (computeSackFoodTransfer); payment = a prosperity BAND-STEP debit on the buyer + a bounded non-zero-sum seller income nudge (the sim's prosperity vocabulary — NO conserved-coin primitive, per the f3cf639e ruling X/Z). Debt-free (no obligation), no legitimacy spent (a sale is not charity). The broad shortage→surplus enumeration is deferred to the acquisition-ladder mover (W-DOCTRINE, ruling Y).

LIVE (E1b, §3.4): GIVE_AS_CREDIT mints a maturity-bearing kind:credit obligation; at maturity the debtor repays (trust, debt clears) or defaults (grievance ratchet = casus-belli seam + the lender's hardened heart via lendAppetite).

LIVE (E1d, design A4): the per-pair GIVE-STREAM warms a corridor — a dwell-bounded tradeOverture sub-ledger (the merchantAppetite idiom, drop-when-cold ⇒ byte-neutral) rises on each gift the pair exchanges. When warmth crosses the open threshold (with dwell) the giver opens an OVERTURE: a byte-neutral trust-nudge into the EXISTING neutral_to_trade_partner evolution rule (NEVER an autonomous edge — the f3cf639e ruling Y). Initiation routes through authorityFor (auto-applies under routine; withheld under dm_only/recommendations — ruling Z). The tradeFlow node-tally is superseded (per-node cannot express per-corridor warmth).

LIVE (E1c): "people, not goods" — refugeAcceptance opens a host POSTURE (give-side motive only; cost priced downstream by M4 congestion), written to the drop-when-empty refugePostures sub-ledger, READ in migrationKernel.buildDestinationCandidate as the refugePosture01 axis on destinationScore. Court successions per faction, per sim-decade

The cadence dial targets "a succession per faction every few sim-years, NEITHER stasis NOR churn." A few years is roughly one every 2.5 to 6.5 years, i.e. 1.5 to 4 per decade. The 104-week post-succession cooldown caps the ceiling; the anti-stasis floor keeps it above zero. Below the floor reads as a frozen court; above the ceiling reads as churn.

Contests are hard-capped at two live per settlement (CONTESTS_PER_SETTLEMENT_CAP), with a 0.04 per-advance discovery base. A healthy world has occasional live rivalries, not a permanent brawl in every town: mean well under the cap, but non-trivially above zero. The structural ceiling is 2; the ratified watch-band is 0.05 to 1.2.
Share of live positive bonds at or near the full-mark cap
fraction of active bonds at >= 0.9 of the cap

A bond mints half a mark (BOND_MINT_SEV 0.5), stacks additively, is clamped to a full mark (BOND_MAX_SEV 1.0), and fades on a ~3-year half-life (BOND_HALF_LIFE_WEEKS 156). If most live bonds sit maxed, the mint is too generous or decay too slow (everyone is everyone else best friend); if almost none approach the cap, bonds never deepen. The ratified watch-band is 5 to 40 percent of live bonds near the cap.
Festivals actually observed per settlement, per year

A festival window opens once per year, but hard stressors (plague, famine, war, occupation) and a Subsistence economy (SKIP_PROSPERITY_RANK_MAX 0) cancel it. A healthy world celebrates most years with some cancellations, so the observed rate sits below the once-per-year ceiling of 1.0: a ratified 0.55 to 0.98. A rate near 1.0 means nothing is ever hard enough to cancel; a low rate means the world is in permanent crisis.
Share of observed festivals that score a triumph

The success model centres on BASE 0.55 with a triumph reached when the seed draw beats score+TRIUMPH_OFFSET (-0.25), i.e. roughly the lower ~30 percent of draws at a middling economy, shifted by prosperity and memory. Triumphs should be a real minority, not routine and not vanishing: a ratified 0.15 to 0.45.
Share of qualifying gifts that deposit a lasting gratitude bond
fraction of gifts that mint above the obligation floor

Gratitude scales with need relieved and the giver sacrifice (the widow-mite rule: GRATITUDE_MITE 1.0 lets a costly gift bind up to twice a costless one), with a small lift for gifts through a named tie (TIE_BIND 0.25), clamped to a full mark. Most meaningful gifts should leave a mark, but not every trivial transfer: a ratified 40 to 90 percent mint rate above the obligation floor.
Mean severity of a freshly minted gratitude bond

Minted severity is clamped to [0, 1] and driven by need, sacrifice, and tie. A mean near 1.0 means every gift is a life-debt (the mint is too hot); a mean near 0 means gratitude never accumulates. The ratified watch-band is a mean of 0.20 to 0.70, leaving headroom for the exceptional widow-mite gift to stand out.
Annual share of an occupied settlement population that flees
fraction of population per year, occupied settlements

Flight is emergent: occupation presses the monthly population rate down by 0.016, and crisis-flight settlements are capped at 18 percent of population per interval (versus 5.5 percent normal). The design law is rescuable, not annihilated, so a bounded but visible bleed is right: a ratified 2 to 15 percent per year. The 18 percent per-interval severe cap is the hard structural ceiling this band sits under; below 2 percent, an occupied town does not visibly bleed at all.
Coup-success swing between a prosperous seat and a hollowed one
delta in coup-success probability across the prosperity spectrum

The economic term shifts the incumbent hold-chance by (economic_capacity - 50) / 400, i.e. plus or minus 0.125 at the extremes. A prosperous seat holds; a hollowed treasury falls. The observed coup-success-rate difference between the richest and poorest seats should approach but not exceed twice that span (~0.25). A swing near 0 means prosperity does not matter; a ratified watch-band of 0.05 to 0.25 keeps the economy load-bearing without deciding every coup.

pressure_event, faction_competition, stressor_escalation, and relationship_evolution escalate to proposal on severity alone and never consult majorChangesRequireProposal. Setting the flag OFF (e.g. dramatic_campaign) does NOT make these auto, unlike the proposal-gated families. RESOLVED BY DESIGN (Phase 5.5 CL-0, §11): the severity-only behavior IS these families’ per-domain LEGACY DEFAULT, encoded exactly — under politicalAutonomy routine (flag on) AND full (flag off) they keep escalating on severity, byte-identically to the pre-CL0 engine. The new dm_only/recommendations modes force them (and every other candidate family) to proposal via authorityFor. Behavior under legacy inputs remains unchanged.
A refugee wave that moves >=8% of a source population redraws two settlements; that is a new premise, not an implied consequence.
A hard trade-dependency (strength ~0.73+) failing is a structural shock to the dependent settlement; a DM may want to reshape it.
A major population swing is a premise about the settlement’s scale; gated when the flag is on.
A settlement crossing a tier boundary under severe pressure restructures its whole profile; gated above the magnitude threshold.

A tier boundary crossing (tierCandidate, candidateType tier_promotion / tier_demotion) honors majorChangesRequireProposal, consistent with resource_depletion in the same module: it stays a DM proposal under the conservative default (flag on) and auto-applies only when a campaign opts out of proposal gating (flag off, e.g. dramatic_campaign).
An institution being founded or dissolved is a standing-order change to the settlement; gated above the magnitude threshold.

W-LIFECYCLE: a first-class settlement dying for good (its digest cell kept, its status a remnant) is the strongest premise the sim can introduce — the DM sees it coming across the extended terminal dwell and can force or veto. Honors majorChangesRequireProposal (the tier_change precedent), forced to proposal under dm_only/recommendations via authorityFor.

W-LIFECYCLE: a remnant re-founded as a living thorp is a structural roster change (a new premise about the world), the death lane's twin — gated on the same flag, forced to proposal under dm_only/recommendations via authorityFor.
High-pressure emergent events escalate to proposal on pressure score alone; this gate predates majorChangesRequireProposal.
Faction power shifts escalate to proposal on severity thresholds, independent of the flag.
Severe stressors escalate to proposal on severity alone; this gate predates the flag.
Major relationship transitions escalate to proposal on severity alone, independent of the flag.

A faction capture escalates at severity >= 0.68; a new or cleared criminal suppression always asks approval, while continuation of an already-approved live suppression is automatic. All are independent of the proposal flag. (institutionCandidate)
A faction contesting a rival’s power basis escalates to proposal at severity >= 0.7, independent of the flag. (rivalryOrExhaustionCandidate)

A SECOND, distinct stressor gate (stressorCandidate, the pressure-born birth path) escalates to proposal when pressure.score >= 0.78 OR the type is occupation/magic_deadzone/siege/coup_detat, independent of the flag. Distinct from stressor_escalation, which is the severity-driven escalation of an EXISTING stressor.

The defect / sabotage / seek_promotion / undermine_rival NPC action families are FORCED to proposal regardless of computed severity (the `|| [...].includes(actionFamily)` short-circuit in candidateForAction). These are adversarial moves a DM should always be offered a veto on; they never auto-apply.
A government challenge (governmentChallenge) emits a bare applyMode: 'proposal'. Changing a settlement’s government is a new premise; it is unconditionally offered to the DM.

Every diplomatic relabel built through labelProposal emits a bare applyMode: "proposal". A visible relationship label flip (neutral->rival, allied, vassal rebellion, etc.) is a new premise and is unconditionally offered to the DM. Distinct from relationship_evolution, which is the severity-gated internal-drift path.

WR-0c: publicly repudiating a live non-aggression pact lifts every treaty restraint and creates a full treaty_default casus. It is an actor-initiated campaign premise and the realm verb lane always stages it as a proposal; no autonomy flag or severity threshold may auto-apply it.

WR-10 (amendment S): a settlement changes hands. Selling a steading or a settled vassalage moves sovereignty without a siege — the buyer inherits a holding, the sold town inherits a grievance against the court that traded it, and the realm map means something different afterwards. That is an actor-initiated campaign PREMISE, not the bounded consequence of one the DM already accepted, so the realm verb lane stages it unconditionally as a proposal and no autonomy flag or severity threshold may auto-apply it (the treaty_breached precedent, whose gate line this entry shares because the realm-verb lane has exactly one mint).

strategyCandidate emits applyMode: proposal ? 'proposal' : 'auto'. Only the sue_for_peace move passes a `proposal` (it pulls a relationship label-change lever, which is itself always-proposal); every other move (deploy / defend / hold / return_home) passes no proposal and stays auto. The split is structural to the move, not flag- or severity-driven.
Conquest is the resolution of a siege that already broke. The siege is the gated premise; the occupation that follows is its bounded consequence.
Resistance/stabilization/burden transitions of an existing occupation are the mechanical unwinding of a conquest the DM already saw.
Vassalization is the terminal state of an occupation that has run its course; it is implied by the conquest, not a new premise.

How an occupier means to hold a town it already holds is a policy of the same court, not a change of hands; it is asked only when the occupation climbs to a rung where the yield question becomes real.
A long goal crossing its culmination threshold is the payoff of progress the DM watched accrue tick by tick; the ascendance is its bounded consequence.
Trade-war conditions are the bounded propagation of an opt-in war-layer premise the DM enabled.

A successful coup is the resolution of a coup stressor the DM already saw building; it auto-applies UNLESS the player has locked the governing faction, on which separate axis it escalates to proposal.

W-CONVERGENCE: a foreign power committing an army to a settlement's internal (coup) contest is an ACTOR-INITIATED major. The autonomous mover mints directly under legacy routine/full (byte-identical — the feature is dark by default) and routes its legacy 'auto' through authorityFor, which forces 'proposal' under dm_only/recommendations and routine-with-major-approval (the coup_succeeded precedent, escalating on the autonomy mode not a lock).

W-NAVY: a navy throwing a blockade across a hostile port's sea approaches is a siege from the water — the siege-initiation twin, an ACTOR-INITIATED major. The autonomous mover mints directly under legacy routine/full (byte-identical — the feature is dark by default) and routes its legacy 'auto' through authorityFor, which forces 'proposal' under dm_only/recommendations and routine-with-major-approval (the intervention_ordered precedent).
